newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks say tax probe threatens secrecy code.
newsitem.headline: German banks say tax probe threatens secrecy code.

text.p: German banks launched a protest Friday against successive raids on their premises by tax officials in recent years, saying the actions had made the concept of client confidentiality meaningless.

The German Banking Association in Cologne said investigators were increasingly looking into the internal accounts of banks in order to build up information on customers and passing on their discoveries to tax authorities.
"If this implementation ... continues to proceed in this way, then the authorities have undermined banking secrecy," association spokesman Oliver Wolfram told Reuters.
A German Finance Ministry spokesman said a clause in a financial markets law enacted in 1993 supported the activities of tax authorities.
"The banks were involved in preparing that law," the spokesman said. He also denied that the actions violated bank secrecy codes.

While German tax officials remain barred by law from gaining direct access to an account that has been opened in the regular way, where the holder is clearly identifiable, internal bank transactions are not covered in that regulation.
Germany's depleted public coffers have fuelled aggressive action to track down tax evaders in the past few years.

Tax officials have raided hundreds of German bank branches in the past two and a half years over allegations that staff abetted tax evasion by helping clients shift funds to hard-to-trace accounts in Luxembourg.
The nationwide probe followed the exodus of billions of marks to Luxembourg and other tax havens after Germany slapped a 30 percent withholding tax on interest income in 1994.
Moving funds abroad to avoid that tax is not illegal but failing to report interest income to fiscal authorities in Germany is in breach of the law.
